medium.titulo: Should You Switch to GPT-6.1 Sol? The Real Cost vs GPT-6 Sol and Claude
medium.resumo: Same $2/$10 sticker, half-price cached input. The math at real agent volumes vs GPT-6 Sol, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.
medium.conteudo_html:
Same $2/$10 sticker, half-price cached input. The math at real agent volumes vs GPT-6 Sol, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.

GPT-6 Sol is one week old. You may have only just finished migrating to it.

Now OpenAI has shipped GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay (29 September 2026). It’s live in the API as gpt-6.1-sol and in ChatGPT Work and Codex.

So the obvious question comes back: do you change the model string again? And if you’re on Claude, is this the week you move?

I skipped the launch charts and did the per-token arithmetic from the published price pages. Here’s what it says.

What changed, and what didn’t

The headline prices stayed the same. GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, exactly like GPT-6 Sol.

One line changed: cached input dropped from $0.20 to $0.10 per million. That’s 5% of the uncached rate, down from 10%.

Everything else on the model page matches the old one:

  • Cache writes: $2.50 per million (1.25x input)
  • Prompts over 272K input tokens: 2x input and cache rates, 1.5x output, for the whole request
  • Batch and Flex: 50% off. Fast mode: 2x
  • 1,050,000-token context, 128,000 max output

Two things aren’t new, whatever your timeline says. Prompt caching isn’t a new feature, and cheaper cache reads are a price cut, not a new capability. Anthropic already charges $0.20 for Opus 5.5 cache hits. OpenAI has now gone below that.

Where to get it today: ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, and the API. It’s not in regular ChatGPT Chat yet. A GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast tier with up to 8x faster generation in Codex arrives “in the coming days,” per OpenAI. I haven’t seen a price for it, so I’m leaving it out of the math.

The price table, side by side

All prices are per million tokens, standard tier, from each vendor’s own pricing page.

GPT-6.1 Sol: $2 input · $0.10 cached input · $2.50 cache write · $10 output

GPT-6 Sol: $2 input · $0.20 cached input · $2.50 cache write · $10 output

Claude Sonnet 5.5: $2 input · $0.20 cached input · $2.50 cache write (5-min) · $10 output

Claude Opus 5.5: $4 input · $0.20 cached input · $5 cache write (5-min) · $20 output

GPT-6 Astra: $10 input · $1 cached input · $12.50 cache write · $50 output

Two patterns stand out once they’re side by side.

Up to 272K tokens, GPT-6.1 Sol is exactly half of Opus 5.5 on every line. Input, cached input, cache writes, output: all 50%.

GPT-6.1 Sol and Sonnet 5.5 differ on only one line, cached input. Same input, same output, same 5-minute write price.

The long-context rules are different, though. OpenAI surcharges any request over 272K input tokens. Anthropic says Claude 4.6 and later bill the full 1M window at standard rates.

These workloads are my own examples. Swap in the token counts from your own logs. The prices are the published ones above.

Say it runs 2 billion input tokens a month, 90% of them cache hits, plus 50 million output tokens. Agent loops resend the same system prompt, tool schemas and repo context on every turn, so input dwarfs output.

To be pessimistic, I bill the uncached 10% at the cache-write rate.

Moving from 6 to 6.1 saves $180 a month here, about 13%. That’s real money, but it isn’t a budget revolution. The saving comes only from the cached slice. Output, which is often the biggest line, costs exactly what it did.

At a 95% hit rate the saving grows. At 50% it mostly disappears. Log your cache hit rate before you celebrate.

The arithmetic at real volumes

Here it’s 300M uncached input and 30M output a month: one-off PDFs, tickets, extractions.

  • GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Sol, Sonnet 5.5: 300M × $2 + 30M × $10 = $900
  • Opus 5.5: $1,200 + $600 = $1,800
  • Astra: $3,000 + $1,500 = $4,500

Batch halves any of these if you can wait.

On price, 6.1 changes nothing for this workload. If you switch, do it because the output is better, not because the bill is.

Now take a 400K-token prompt with 8K tokens out. Think “here’s the whole repo” or “here’s the data room”.

With no cache, per call:

At 1,000 calls a month, that’s $1,720 vs $880 vs $1,760. Past 272K, OpenAI’s surcharge makes GPT-6.1 Sol cost about the same as Opus 5.5 and roughly twice as much as Sonnet 5.5 per token.

If the prefix is cached (ignoring the first write), the gap nearly closes. It’s $0.20 a call on GPT-6.1 Sol (the $0.10 cache rate doubles to $0.20), $0.16 on Sonnet 5.5, $0.24 on Opus 5.5, and $0.28 on old GPT-6 Sol.

The lesson: keep OpenAI prompts under 272K, or cache them.

All of this is per token, not per task.

Tokenizers differ between vendors, so the same text isn’t the same number of tokens on Claude and on OpenAI. Anthropic’s own pricing page says its tokenizer for Claude 4.7 and later produces about 30% more tokens for the same text than its older one.

Models also think for different lengths. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 costs about 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads because it uses fewer tokens per task.

So the real break-even for Opus 5.5 is simple to state and hard to guess. It has to finish your task in half the tokens GPT-6.1 Sol needs. Only your traces can tell you whether it does.

What OpenAI claims (and how to read it)

Everything in this section is OpenAI’s own benchmarks, run in its environment. It’s useful as a hint, not proof.

  • DeepSWE v1.1: OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost, and beats GPT-6 Sol’s best score by 6.4 points at lower effort.
  • AutomationBench: 2.2 points above Opus 5.5 at medium effort, at roughly a third of the cost, per OpenAI.
  • OSWorld 2.0 (offline): 7 points over GPT-6 Sol at max effort, and within 2.1 points of Astra.
  • Terminal-Bench Science 0.1: OpenAI puts the average cost per task at $5.47, against $23.21 for Opus 5.5 and $23.80 for Astra. It also says Astra still scores highest (68.1%) and should be used for the hardest science work.

Anthropic’s launch pages make their own cross-vendor cost-per-task claims too. Sonnet 5.5’s page compares it with the older GPT-6 Sol, not with 6.1.

The comparisons in the launch posts are vendor-run, so treat any “X destroys Y” post with suspicion until someone runs both on the same harness.

Should you switch from GPT-6 Sol?

Mostly yes. It’s the cheapest upgrade you’ll get this month. The price is the same or lower on every line, and OpenAI says the model is better. But check these before you flip it in production:

  • reasoning.effort: none and minimal are gone. GPT-6 Sol supported none. 6.1 starts at low, with medium as the default. If you depended on none for fast, cheap calls, your latency and token counts will change.
  • Tool calling in Chat Completions is gone. GPT-6 Sol allowed function calling in Chat Completions with effort none. For 6.1, the docs say to use the Responses API for tool calling. Chat Completions works only without tools.
  • Check the tool list. When I read it this morning, the 6.1 model page listed file search, code interpreter, hosted shell, apply patch, skills, computer use and MCP. It didn’t list web search or tool search, which the GPT-6 Sol page does. If your agent depends on either, confirm before you migrate.
  • EU data residency is supported, but Fast mode isn’t available with it.

Hold off, or A/B first, if your workload is mostly uncached (the saving is zero) or you have a hand-tuned eval suite on GPT-6 Sol. One week is a short time to have tuned prompts around a model. Rerun them anyway.

Should you switch from Claude?

From Sonnet 5.5: the per-token bill is nearly identical. The only price difference under 272K is cached input, $0.10 vs $0.20. Over 272K, Sonnet 5.5 is cheaper per token. Switch only if GPT-6.1 Sol wins on quality in your own evals, or if you want OpenAI’s hosted tools and Codex. Price alone isn’t a reason.

From Opus 5.5: here the price gap is real. GPT-6.1 Sol is half the per-token price on every line. It’s worth an A/B test for:

  • Business-workflow agents and document Q&A, where OpenAI claims its biggest wins over Opus 5.5 (again, OpenAI’s claims)
  • High-volume, cache-heavy loops where the cache-read gap compounds

Stay on Opus 5.5 if Claude Code is your harness and it’s working, if your tasks are long and open-ended, or if your traces show Opus finishing in far fewer tokens. Rewriting a working stack to halve a line item is a trade, not a win.

Big-context work without caching: Sonnet 5.5 is the cheaper per-token choice, because Claude doesn’t charge extra past 272K.

The hardest tasks: OpenAI itself says Astra still leads on the hardest science. For rare, expensive-if-wrong jobs, escalate to Astra or Opus 5.5 instead of forcing everything through a mid-tier model.

Bottom line

If you’re on gpt-6-sol, change the string to gpt-6.1-sol, check the effort and Chat Completions changes, and watch your cache hit rate. The bill drops only as much as your cache hit rate allows.

If you’re on Claude, this is an A/B test, not an emergency. Against Opus 5.5 the per-token math is 2:1. Against Sonnet 5.5 it’s a coin flip decided by caching and prompt size.

Either way, the rule hasn’t changed: pick the cheapest model that actually finishes the job, and prove it with your own traces.

I write practical notes on picking and running AI models at kylet.se.

medium.resumo: Derive values with computed, react to changes with watch.
medium.conteudo_html:
Derive values with computed, react to changes with watch.

Both respond to reactive changes, but they answer different questions. Mixing them up leads to clunky code.

computed — derive a new value

Use it when a value is calculated from other state. It’s cached and only re-runs when its dependencies change.

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
const first = ref('Ada')
const last = ref('Lovelace')
const fullName = computed(() => `${first.value} ${last.value}`)
console.log(fullName.value) // "Ada Lovelace"

watch — run a side effect

Use it when a change should trigger an action — fetching data, logging, syncing to storage.

import { ref, watch } from 'vue'
const query = ref('')
watch(query, (newVal, oldVal) => {
  console.log(`searching for ${newVal}`)
  // fetchResults(newVal)
})

The rule of thumb

Returning a value for the template? → computed
Performing an action in response to a change? → watch

If you find yourself manually assigning to a ref inside a watch just to derive a value, you probably want computed instead.

TL;DR: computed produces a cached derived value; watch runs side effects when something changes.

Next time you reach for watch, ask “am I just calculating something?” — if so, computed is cleaner.

medium.titulo: Why I Didn’t Pick the Most Popular Framework for My Game Site
medium.resumo: I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.
medium.conteudo_html:
I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.

Before I started building my game collection site, I spent a long time agonizing over the tech stack.

Next.js 14 is the popular choice right now. App Router + SSG looks perfect for a content site. Vue 3 + Vite is known for being lightweight — smaller first-load JS, faster builds. Both have good arguments. There are plenty of comparison articles online, but reading them only made me more indecisive. They all compared specs, but none of them told me how to choose given my constraints.

So I stopped reading and started building. Same MVP, two stacks, one after the other. Let the data decide.

What I found was something more important than the stack itself.

What I Actually Cared About

Most people start tech selection by comparing feature lists. But feature lists are infinite. What actually constrains you are just a few things. I wrote down three hard constraints:

One: SEO had to work. Most traffic for a game site comes from search engines. Game detail pages must be crawlable. This wasn’t “nice to have” — it was mandatory.

Two: First load had to be fast. LCP under 2.5s on mobile 4G. Users have only a few seconds of patience. Slow means gone.

Three: The game iframe couldn’t block the main thread. While browsing the list page, no game runtime code should load. I’ll come back to this point, because it turned out to be the real key.

These three constraints ended up driving my entire decision.

Day 1: Next.js Version — Static Export Taught Me a Lesson

I built the homepage, category pages, and game runtime page with Next.js 14 App Router, using output: 'export' for pure static export, deployed to Vercel.

Homepage and category pages generated HTML correctly. But /play/[id] all returned 404.

After digging in: App Router with output: 'export' doesn’t support dynamic routes by default unless you explicitly define generateStaticParams. This is heavily discussed in the community; developers have reported that “the latest Next.js App Router doesn’t support dynamic routes with static generation.”

Worse, even after defining generateStaticParams, all game IDs have to be pre-generated at build time. If the game count grows to hundreds, every new game triggers a full rebuild, and CI time grows exponentially.

I tried @falsefoundation/next-dynamic-exports, which supports dynamic routes by generating fallback pages, but it requires web server rewrite rules, adding deployment complexity.

Then I tried a different approach: turn the game runtime page from a dynamic route into a client-rendered static shell — the /play page reads the game ID via useSearchParams after loading. This bypasses the generateStaticParams limitation, but the game runtime page is no longer prerendered, so SEO suffers. My trade-off: the game runtime page has low SEO value anyway (users arrive from the detail page), so it’s acceptable.

Next.js version data: Homepage LCP 1.2s (mobile 4G throttling), first-load JS ~85KB (gzip), build time 12s.

（When publishing to Medium, embed the code snippets above via Gist to avoid formatting issues. Same for the rest of this article.）

Day 2: Vue 3 + Vite Version — Genuinely Lightweight

Vue’s dev experience was excellent. Vite cold start under 1 second, hot updates nearly imperceptible, build time only 6 seconds — half of Next.js. First-load JS ~50KB, nearly 40% less.

But SEO became a problem.

Vue + Vite defaults to SPA. The homepage and category pages only contain <div id="app"></div> in the HTML — crawlers see no content. The solution was to install vite-plugin-seo-prerender, which prerenders the SPA into static HTML files at build time.

Configuration is simple:

// vite.config.ts
import seoPrerender from 'vite-plugin-seo-prerender'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    seoPrerender({
      routes: ['/', '/games/puzzle', '/games/sports']
    })
  ]
})

But the plugin has a limitation: it’s only suitable for generating static HTML for a small number of pages. If the game count grows to hundreds, every game detail page needs prerendering, and build time becomes uncontrollable.

Another option is Nuxt 3, Vue’s meta-framework with built-in SSG. But that introduces another framework, contradicting the “lightweight” goal.

Vue version data: Homepage LCP 1.5s (after prerendering), first-load JS ~50KB (gzip), build time 6s.

Day 3: A Counterintuitive Finding

After both versions were running, I did one thing: recorded the full timeline from homepage to clicking “Start Game” using Chrome DevTools Performance panel on both.

Something counterintuitive came up: the performance difference between the two versions was far smaller than I expected.

The Next.js version had 35KB more first-load JS, but on 4G that’s about 200ms of download time. The real time sink while browsing the list page wasn’t the framework’s JS size — it was the game iframe initialization.

In the default implementation, the iframe was initialized when the game detail page mounted. Even if the iframe src pointed to an empty placeholder page, creating the contentWindow and initializing the sandbox environment still consumed main thread time. On a Moto G Power, that single operation took about 400ms.

The correct approach is the facade pattern: render only a lightweight static placeholder (thumbnail + play button) before the iframe mounts, and inject the actual iframe only when the user clicks “Start.” This matches Lighthouse’s recommendation for deferring third-party resources.

There’s a Next.js static wiki case in the DEV community that uses the facade pattern to move a YouTube iframe from hydration-time mount to click-time load, bringing mobile TBT down from destructive levels to acceptable.

This means: the framework choice’s impact on first-load performance is far smaller than the iframe initialization strategy’s impact.

I wrote this down because it directly changed my selection criteria. Before, I was comparing “whose first-load JS is smaller.” Now I was comparing “who makes the facade pattern easier to implement.”

Final Choice: Hybrid Architecture

Based on the three-day comparison, I made these decisions:

Static content pages (homepage, category pages, detail pages) use Next.js SSG.SEO works out of the box, no extra plugins. Dynamic routes have limitations, but the game detail page ID count is manageable (only 6 games initially). If the game count grows to 200+, a Headless CMS with ISR can be introduced, but that requires a server and breaks the zero-backend constraint.

The game runtime page uses an independent client-rendered shell. The game runtime page has low SEO value and doesn’t need prerendering. Use next/dynamicwith ssr: false to lazy-load the game iframe component, facade pattern: initialize the iframe only after the user clicks “Start.”

Here’s the concrete implementation:

// components/GameLauncher.tsx
'use client'
import { useState } from 'react'
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic'

const GameIframe = dynamic(() => import('./GameIframe'), {
  ssr: false,
  loading: () => <div className="h-full bg-zinc-900 animate-pulse" />
})

export default function GameLauncher({ game }) {
  const [started, setStarted] = useState(false)

  if (!started) {
    return (
      <button
        onClick={() => setStarted(true)}
        className="relative w-full aspect-video rounded-lg overflow-hidden"
      >
        <img src={game.thumbnail} alt={game.title} className="w-full h-full object-cover" />
        <div className="absolute inset-0 flex items-center justify-center">
          <svg width="64" height="64" viewBox="0 0 64 64">
            <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="30" fill="rgba(0,0,0,0.6)" />
            <polygon points="26,20 26,44 46,32" fill="white" />
          </svg>
        </div>
      </button>
    )
  }

  return <GameIframe src={game.entry} gameId={game.id} />
}

ssr: false ensures the iframe component isn’t bundled into the HTML during server rendering, and only loads from the client after the user clicks. This matches Next.js’s official lazy-loading advice: for heavy components that don’t participate in SSR, use next/dynamic with ssr: false to reduce the initial bundle.

The Vue version wasn’t maintained. It builds faster and has a smaller bundle, but SEO needs extra plugins, and if the game count grows, the prerendering solution’s scalability is worse than Next.js’s SSG system.

Data Comparison

MetricNext.js 14Vue 3 + ViteFirst-load JS (gzip)~85KB~50KBHomepage LCP (4G)1.2s1.5s (after prerendering)Build time12s6sDynamic route supportNeeds generateStaticParamsBuilt-inSEOOut of the boxNeeds extra pluginsGame runtime lazy loadnext/dynamic native supportManual implementation

Test conditions: MacBook Pro M1 build, iPhone 12 + Chrome DevTools 4G throttling, 10 runs each, median.

Note a counterintuitive result: Vue’s LCP was actually slower than Next.js after prerendering. The reason is that vite-plugin-seo-prerender still includes the full Vue runtime in the generated HTML, while Next.js SSG outputs cleaner HTML with lower hydration cost. This shows that “smaller first-load JS” doesn’t equal “faster first load.”

（When publishing to Medium, turn this table into an image, since Medium doesn’t handle Markdown tables well.）

Trade-offs

Next.js build time is longer. 12s vs 6s. Every new game requires a rebuild. If the game count reaches 50, build time could exceed 30 seconds.

The Vue version was abandoned. It has better dev experience and a smaller bundle, but needs extra work on SEO and scalability. If your game site doesn’t need SEO — an internal tool or pure entertainment site — Vue + Vite is the better choice.

The hybrid architecture adds complexity. Static pages and the runtime page use different rendering strategies, requiring understanding of two sets of logic.

Unresolved

If the game count exceeds 100, generateStaticParams full pre-generation becomes a bottleneck, requiring ISR or a Headless CMS — but that’s no longer zero-backend.

I didn’t dig deep into Vue’s prerendering solution. vite-plugin-prerender-staticsupports multi-route generation and SEO meta tags, which might be enough if the game count is small.

Astro is another direction worth watching. A developer built a 50+ game site with Astro + vanilla JS, keeping the JS bundle under 100KB gzip and emphasizing “each game only loads the JavaScript it actually needs.” This approach is in the same spirit as the facade pattern. If you’re in the selection phase, it’s worth half a day to look into.

What This Means for You

If you’re making a similar tech decision, here’s my advice:

Define your hard constraints first, then look at frameworks. If your constraints are the same as mine (SEO + first load + iframe not blocking the main thread), the real decision point isn’t “Next.js or Vue” — it’s “how to implement the facade pattern.” The framework is just a container. Pick one whose downsides you can live with.

Don’t just look at first-load JS size. The Vue version was 35KB smaller, but its LCP after prerendering was actually slower. The relationship between size and performance is more complex than a spec sheet suggests.

Building both versions for three days is more useful than reading thirty comparison articles. The point of this article isn’t to tell you to pick Next.js. It’s to show you how to reach your own conclusion.

Full Code

Both MVP versions are organized, including Next.js and Vue comparison branches. The test data comes from a local environment. If you get different results on real hardware, I’d love to hear about it.

This article is based on my own project’s selection notes. AI was used only for grammar checking and structural suggestions; the technical judgments and test data come from actual runs.

corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quarta-feira | 30 de setembro de 2026

Um caso que gerou polêmica foi o de uma criança que correu as Dez Milhas Garoto, uma prova de 16 km, de forma ilegal. A criança utilizou um número de peito da “Garotada”, a corrida infantil do evento, que era para a distância de 400 metros. A própria organização da prova estabelece faixas etárias para as corridas infantis: 200m (6-7 anos), 400m (8-9 anos), meia milha (10-13 anos) e uma milha (14-17 anos). A atitude vai contra a Norma 12 da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt), que define as distâncias máximas permitidas por idade. Para correr 10 milhas, seria necessário ter entre 18 e 19 anos completos no ano da prova (categoria Sub-20). O fato levanta um debate sobre a responsabilidade dos pais que incentivam seus filhos a não seguirem as regras, colocando em risco a saúde da criança e ensinando um mau exemplo desde cedo.

Inscrições para a São Silvestre abrem hoje

Chegou a hora! As inscrições para a 101ª edição da Corrida Internacional de São Silvestre abrem para o público geral hoje, 30 de setembro, a partir das 10h da manhã. Os interessados devem acessar o site oficial, saosilvestre.com.br. É importante ficar atento e não cair em golpes de sites falsos. Para quem é de fora de São Paulo, agora é o momento de garantir a inscrição para depois planejar a compra de passagens e hospedagem.

Vem aí a 10ª edição da Maratona da Muralha

A Maratona da Muralha, uma das provas mais singulares do Brasil, terá sua 10ª edição comemorativa em 15 de agosto de 2027. O percurso será “Down”, descendo de Visconde de Mauá para Penedo (RJ). A prova é conhecida por sua energia e por reunir todos os 42 corredores na largada. As inscrições para o lote único abrem no dia 6 de outubro de 2026, precisamente às 19h42min19s. Aqueles que completaram todas as edições receberão um número de peito preto vitalício, que poderá ser passado para seus filhos.

Maratona de Boston divulga tempo de corte para 2027

A Maratona de Boston anunciou oficialmente o tempo de corte para a edição de 2027. Para garantir a vaga, os corredores precisaram ser 5 minutos e 17 segundos mais rápidos que o tempo de qualificação exigido para sua faixa etária. Com isso, mais de 8 mil corredores qualificados ficaram de fora da prova. Como novidade, a organização sorteará mil vagas entre aqueles que não conseguiram a vaga pelo tempo de corte.

NYRR impõe restrições a clubes na Maratona de Nova York

A New York Road Runners (NYRR), organizadora da Maratona de Nova York, decidiu restringir as ações dos clubes de corrida durante o evento deste ano. Em um comunicado, a organização proibiu a exibição de banners de marcas que não sejam patrocinadoras oficiais, o uso de giz no chão, o consumo de álcool, canhões de confete, drones e outras atividades nas zonas de torcida. A medida visa organizar a festa popular que acontece ao longo do percurso, mas a dúvida é se conseguirão fiscalizar e fazer cumprir as novas regras, já que a prova reúne mais de um milhão de pessoas nas ruas.

A medalha-mandala do Circuito Brasil Gigante

A impressionante medalha em formato de mandala do Circuito Brasil Gigante é produzida pela Metalvest, uma empresa especializada em medalhas e troféus de alta qualidade. Com quase meio quilo, a peça é um exemplo do trabalho diferenciado da empresa, que também é responsável pelas medalhas de grandes eventos como as do Circuito Athenas e o Troféu Brasil de Atletismo. Se você é organizador e busca uma premiação especial para seu evento, vale a pena conhecer o trabalho deles.
